questions.q: By default, when you call session.udf.register() or the @udf decorator without is_permanent=True, what kind of UDF do you get?
options: A temporary UDF, scoped to the current session
An error -- is_permanent must always be specified
A permanent UDF that persists forever
A UDF that only works for one query, then is deleted
questions.explain: Temporary is the default, lasting only for the current session -- correct for development and ad hoc work. Permanent requires explicitly passing is_permanent=True plus a stage_location.

questions.q: What does a permanent UDF specifically require that a temporary UDF does not?
options: A warehouse size specification
A stage_location, since the Python file and dependencies need to be uploaded somewhere durable
A unique database per UDF
A different programming language
questions.explain: Permanent UDFs need a stage_location so Snowflake can durably store the Python file and dependencies -- temporary UDFs don't persist past the session, so they don't need this.

questions.q: Why is an unpinned package version a real production risk specifically for a TEMPORARY UDF?
options: Because dependency resolution happens fresh every time it's registered in a new session, so it can silently pick up a newer package version with no code change
Temporary UDFs always use the oldest available package version
This is not a real risk for temporary UDFs, only permanent ones
Temporary UDFs cannot use any external packages at all
questions.explain: A temporary UDF resolves its package versions fresh at every registration, so an unpinned version can change behavior from one session to the next without any code change -- a real, specific failure mode, not hypothetical.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a Python UDF and a Snowpark stored procedure?
options: A UDF can only return NULL; a stored procedure must return a table
There is no real difference -- they are interchangeable terms
Stored procedures cannot be written in Python, only SQL
A UDF processes data within a query (row/batch at a time); a stored procedure is a standalone callable unit that can run multiple queries and orchestrate steps
questions.explain: A UDF is called inside a query to process values; a stored procedure is its own statement that can run a whole sequence of steps -- which is why it's the natural thing for a Task to call.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a Snowpark stored procedure is a natural fit for a Chapter 8 Task?
options: A Task can call a stored procedure that reads a Stream's changes, transforms them, writes results, and logs outcomes -- all as one schedulable unit, instead of one hardcoded SQL statement
Streams require a stored procedure to function at all
Stored procedures run faster than any SQL statement
Tasks can only call stored procedures, never raw SQL
questions.explain: A Task scheduling a single hardcoded SQL statement is limited; calling a stored procedure lets that scheduled run do considerably more sophisticated, multi-step orchestration.
